newsitem.title: USA: Gibson Greetings seeks Paper Factory buyer.
newsitem.headline: Gibson Greetings seeks Paper Factory buyer.

text.p: Gibson Greetings Inc said Sunday the greeting card company is looking for a buyer for its retail stores unit, The Paper Factory of Wisconsin Inc.

Although the company has said the division is doing well, Gibson president, chairman and chief executive Frank O'Connell told reporters that The Paper Factory does not fit into the company's core business plan.
"We're going to some strategic buyers and basically seeing if we can sell this company," O'Connell said while at a trade show in Chicago.
O'Connell said Cincinnati-based Gibson will not accept a price it does not see as appropriate just to sell the unit. He said key to a deal would be a significant supply agreement with the buyer.
"We do well by selling (to) The Paper Factory (Gibson) products. We're not retailers," O'Connell said.
"We will sell it with a long-term product agreement and continue to make money," he said.
He declined to name possible buyers, but said the company would talk to large players in the retail party goods business.
O'Connell said Gibson, however, is "very aggressive" in looking for possible acquisitions and expects to buy at least one company by the end of the year.
Although Gibson is still mainly targeting mass outlets like supermarkets, its strategy is to become a niche-oriented "entertainment company" as society and families change.
O'Connell said he sees the company buying a smaller alternative card company, such as one focusing specifically on Generation X or making recycled paper cards.
Gibson's Ripple Effects brand of cards, with very direct messages and bold graphics, are very successful, he said.

In retail testing, the company said 25 percent more Ripple Effects were sold than basic greeting cards, and 50 percent more than other alternative cards. In fact, O'Connell said they have sold well with more than just the twenty- and thirty-somethings they were initially designed for.
"We'll either generate more product like that or buy a company," he said.
Overall, the licensing business is also very important to Gibson, O'Connell said.
The company has exclusive rights to hit movies Jurassic Park and Batman & Robin, for example, and O'Connell said it recently signed an agreement for the upcoming Men in Black.
With the exclusive agreements, the company can sell to shops which have deals with the top-selling card company in the United States, Hallmark Cards Inc, or number two American Greetings Corp.
So far, licensing agreements have pulled in 90 percent of revenues from other products sold alongside cards, like toys.

Overall, O'Connell, who joined Gibson last August, sees the industry as behind the times and intends to change that for Gibson. The company has spent $500,000 in the last six months on research, and increased marketing and selling expenses to move out outdated products and deliver new lines.
O'Connell said research firms have found that over the last 10 years, the U.S. card industry has seen at least a percentage point drop in unit volume each year.
"For years (the industry) chased the traditional family," O'Connell said, adding that divorced or single-parent families, and younger generations have been left out.
"Unit volume is down significantly because (the industry is) not contemporary in serving these niches," he said.
((--Chicago newsdesk, 312-408-8787))
